strings.title: Earth and Moon Orbits
strings.subtitle: The Earth and Moon travelling around the Sun, seen from above the north side of Earth's orbital plane (the north ecliptic pole).
strings.latlonHint: North and east are positive; south and west are negative.
strings.latlonError: Enter a latitude from −90 to 90 and a longitude from −180 to 180.
strings.ariaPlan: Animation of the Earth and Moon orbiting the Sun, seen from above
strings.ariaElev: The Earth and Moon seen edge-on
strings.ariaStrip: The Moon's path with Earth's orbit straightened
strings.ariaInset: Close-up of Earth's rotation, day and night
strings.planNote: Seen from above the north ecliptic pole · Earth and Moon both orbit anticlockwise
strings.sectorNote: Each shaded sector covers 1/12 of a year; all have the same area
strings.sizesNote: Sun and Earth not to scale
strings.vernalDir: To the March equinox point (ecliptic longitude 0°) →
strings.elevTitle: ▲ The top view, seen edge-on from its lower edge
strings.elevUpper: Upper ticks: days Earth is behind the Sun
strings.elevLower: Lower ticks: days Earth is in front of the Sun
strings.sideSub: The band under the top view shows the same scene edge-on, seen from the June-solstice side with the same horizontal scale. Dotted lines link the Earth, Moon and Sun in both views. Earth swings between its March equinox position (left) and its September equinox position (right), passing in front of the Sun around the June solstice and behind it around the December solstice. Only the sunlit sides of the Earth and Moon are bright.
strings.whereFront: In front of the Sun, moving {dir}
strings.vxNote: Fastest when passing in front of or behind the Sun
strings.nodeLabel: Angle between the Sun and the Moon's nodes
strings.nodeNote: Below about 17°, eclipses can happen at new or full moon
strings.tiltHint: The Moon's orbit is tilted only 5.1° to Earth's orbital plane, so only the vertical direction is stretched.
strings.stripTitle: The Moon's path with Earth's orbit straightened
strings.stripSub: Earth's orbit is straightened into a line: Earth moves right and the Sun is toward the top. The solid line is the path so far and the dotted line is still to come. The purple band in the top view marks this stretch. Drag sideways to move through time.
strings.stripK: Moon's orbital speed ÷ Earth's orbital speed ≈ {k} → {shape}
strings.shapeCusp: sharp cusps, close to a cycloid
strings.stripNote: The Moon passes on the Sun side (top) around new moon and on the far side (bottom) around full moon. At the real speeds its path only waves and never loops. In this straightened view the path bends away from the Sun near new moon, but Earth's real orbit curves toward the Sun, so the Moon's true path always curves toward the Sun. The Sun pulls on the Moon about 2.2 times as hard as Earth does.
strings.sunLonNote: Direction of the Sun seen from Earth
strings.moonNoRise: Does not rise on this day
strings.insetTitle: Close-up of Earth (rotation, day and night)
strings.rotHint: Set the speed to 1 day/s or less to show {place} and Earth's rotation.
strings.axisNote: Earth's axis stays tilted 23.4° toward the top of the view (ecliptic longitude 90°) all year. Around the June solstice the North Pole leans toward the Sun.
strings.eccHint: A larger eccentricity makes it easier to see Earth speed up near perihelion and slow down near aphelion.
strings.note1: Earth's position comes from solving Kepler's equation with JPL mean orbital elements (J2000, Earth–Moon barycentre). The Moon's position uses the main terms of the lunar theory in J. Meeus, Astronomical Algorithms. Equinox and new/full moon times are accurate to within about half an hour; perihelion and aphelion dates can be off by 1–2 days because of the Moon.
strings.note2: Earth's orbit is nearly a circle (eccentricity 0.0167). The Earth–Moon distance is only about 1/390 of the distance to the Sun, so the Moon's distance is enlarged in the figures.
strings.note3: Press the space bar to play or pause.
